rubric.scale: 0-10 per criterion. 10 minus evidence-backed deductions, then moderation. 9-10 means nothing material to fix. No default mid-point: a criterion with no deductible problem scores 10.

severity_meaning.minor: A selector might notice; unlikely to change a decision alone.
severity_meaning.moderate: A selector would mark the statement down on this.
severity_meaning.major: A published criterion is clearly not met; could decide the outcome.

criteria.name: Academic focus and proportion

main.rule: Share of characters in sentences about the subjects, reading or study. LSE: at least 80% (C-003).

durham.rule: No published percentage for Durham; only a clearly non-academic statement is penalised.

criteria.name: Critical engagement and own views

main.rule: Sentences giving the applicant's own view with a reason, or a stated objection. Named reading with nothing learned is penalised (C-016).

durham.rule: As main, but views must concern economics.

criteria.name: Balance and link between the two subjects

main.rule: Equal weight to philosophy and economics (C-006) and at least one sentence connecting them, as PH311 does (C-023).

durham.name: Fit with Economics
durham.rule: The substitute replaces the main statement for an Economics degree, so its academic content must be about economics.

criteria.name: Fit with the degree as taught and across choices

main.rule: Touches the strands the named programmes teach: economic theory, quantitative methods, logic/argument, ethics or value, philosophy of economics/science. TODO choices are not assessed.

durham.rule: Touches micro/macro theory, data and quantitative methods, applied policy.

criteria.name: Right content in each of the 3 questions, no repetition

main.rule: Q1 motivation and subject knowledge with no career plans; Q2 recent study, not grades; Q3 reflected activities; no repeated material.

durham.rule: As main; careers in Q1 is advisory only (no tier 1 ban for Durham).

criteria.name: Writing and use of space

main.rule: AI-sounding or stock phrasing, list-like writing, length limits.

checks.name: Generic or AI-sounding phrasing (quoted)

calibration.draft_text:
Q1:
I want to study Philosophy and Economics because I am interested in how societies make decisions about money and fairness. My interest in economics began when I read Freakonomics by Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner, which showed me that economics can explain many surprising things in everyday life. I then read Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman, which was about the two systems of thinking and how people make mistakes. I found it very interesting that people are not always rational. I have also been reading The Economist every week, which has helped me keep up with topics like inflation, interest rates and the cost of living crisis. In philosophy I have read some of Mill's Utilitarianism, and I think the idea of the greatest happiness for the greatest number is a useful way of thinking about government policy because it focuses on outcomes. I would like to learn more about how economic models work and how they are used to make policy decisions.

Q2:
Studying IB Economics HL has given me a good understanding of supply and demand, market failure and macroeconomic policy. For my internal assessments I wrote commentaries on news articles about tariffs, subsidies and price controls, which helped me apply theory to real situations. I am predicted a 7 in Economics and a 6 in Mathematics, and I achieved high marks in my mock exams. IB Mathematics Applications and Interpretations has helped me with statistics and graphs, which are important in economics. In Theory of Knowledge we discussed whether economics is a science, and I learned about different ways of knowing. My Extended Essay is about the effect of the sugar tax on soft drink consumption in the UK, and it has taught me how to research and use data.

Q3:
Outside of school I am a member of the debating society, the football team and the school orchestra, where I play the violin. I am also a prefect and I helped organise a charity bake sale that raised money for a local food bank. Last summer I did work experience at an accountancy firm, where I shadowed staff, attended meetings and helped with spreadsheets. These activities have helped me develop teamwork, leadership and communication skills which will help me at university.

calibration.draft_text:
Q1:
Milton Friedman argued in 1953 that an economic theory should be judged by its predictions, not by the realism of its assumptions. I accepted this until I read Amartya Sen's essay "Rational Fools", which argues that the purely economic man is close to being a social moron. Sen's objection unsettled me because Friedman's test cannot catch it: a model of purely selfish agents can predict prices well and still misdescribe people, and that error matters once the same model is used to judge policy. I now think the realism of assumptions matters whenever a model is used to say what people ought to want, not only to forecast what they will do. That question sits between philosophy and economics, which is why I want to study them together. Economics gives me precise tools for asking how incentives shape choices, while philosophy asks whether the preferences we model deserve respect. Reading Michael Sandel on markets crowding out civic norms, I was not convinced by most of his examples, since many are anecdotes. However, the Haifa day-care study he discusses, where a fine for late pick-ups increased lateness, persuaded me that his objection deserves testing rather than dismissal.

Q2:
My Extended Essay asked whether UK minimum wage rises after 2016 reduced youth employment. I expected a clear answer, but the estimates I could reproduce depended on which comparison group I chose, which taught me why econometrics spends so long on identification before it claims anything about causes. IB Philosophy has trained me to reconstruct an argument fairly before attacking it. In a class debate on Rawls I defended the veil of ignorance, but writing up the objection that it assumes extreme risk aversion convinced me that the maximin rule needs more defence than Rawls gives it. Mathematics Analysis and Approaches HL is my hardest subject, and I think it is the most useful, because optimisation is how economists formalise choice and I want to understand a formal model before I criticise it. Theory of Knowledge pushed me on a narrower question: is an economic model a claim about the world or a tool for thinking? My essay argued that it can be both, but only if we state in advance which evidence would count against it, a test I took from Popper and found harder to apply to economics than to physics.

Q3:
Outside school I write a monthly column for our student newsletter that explains one economic idea through a local example, such as why the bus company cut evening routes. Writing for readers who disagree with me taught me to state the strongest version of their view first. I also completed an online course in game theory, and working through repeated prisoner's dilemma problems made me question whether defection is really the rational choice when the game has no fixed end. Working weekends in a café showed me that the owner sets prices by habit rather than marginal cost, which made me more sceptical of textbook pricing models and more curious about behavioural economics.

calibration.draft_text:
Q1:
From a young age I have always been fascinated by the world of economics and money. Economics plays a vital role in today's world, and I have a deep passion for understanding how the economy works. My dream is to become an investment banker in London, and studying at LSE would be the perfect first step on my journey towards this career. Philosophy is also interesting because it makes you think about big questions. I believe this course would allow me to delve into the complexities of the ever-evolving global economy.

Q2:
I am currently studying the IB Diploma and I am predicted 40 points, including a 7 in Economics HL. I have always achieved top grades in my exams and I received an award for the highest mark in my year. My subjects have taught me many skills such as time management, organisation, communication and teamwork. Furthermore, I have honed my analytical skills, which are crucial for success at university. I believe I am a hard-working student who would thrive in this course.

Q3:
I am captain of the rugby team, I play the piano to grade 6, I am a member of the student council and I volunteer at a charity shop on Saturdays. I also enjoy travelling, cooking and going to the gym. These experiences have shaped me into a well-rounded individual. Moreover, they have given me invaluable skills that will help me to embark on my university journey and achieve my dream career in finance.
